structure.title: I. Institutional Setting and Conceptual Framework

observations.statement: The paper states its design as a staggered difference-in-differences with hospital and year fixed effects, defines the coefficient of interest as the change in outcomes after stress-test exposure relative to unexposed hospital-years, and flags interpretation concerns raised by recent staggered-DID econometrics.

The identifying assumption is stated explicitly: a stress test applied to a hospital's relationship bank is treated as exogenous to that hospital's own performance, since bank selection into testing depended on an asset-size threshold rather than on borrower characteristics.
observations.quote: a stress test to an affected bank is exogenous to the performance of the hospital

observations.statement: The paper argues self-selection into relationships with soon-to-be-tested banks is unlikely because the rulemaking timeline was uncertain when most lending relationships were formed and because relationship choice is described as driven by geographic branch proximity rather than anticipation of stress testing; executive interviews are cited as corroboration.

The paper commits to validating the parallel-trends assumption through event-study plots, a formal pre-trend equality test for each outcome, and a sensitivity-bounds approach for any outcome that fails that test, presenting this as part of the identification argument rather than as an afterthought.

The hospital sample is built by combining CMS cost-report data on financial and utilization items, CMS Hospital Compare and HCAHPS data on quality and patient satisfaction, Dealscan loan data, and Federal Reserve stress-test outcomes, linked through hospital-affiliation crosswalks.

The core hospital-year panel spans a fixed multi-year window beginning in the year the paper's key financial variables became consistently defined, with a subset of readmission and mortality outcomes extended one additional year where later data are available.

The sample is restricted to short-term acute-care hospitals and excludes government-owned hospitals such as Veterans Affairs facilities on the stated grounds that they have different incentive structures and direct government support, while noting robustness to including other hospital types.

Treatment exposure is constructed through a manual match of loan-level borrower records to the hospital sample using affiliation data, explicitly handling the case where the borrower on record is a multi-hospital system rather than an individual facility.

A dedicated table reports the yearly counts of newly tested lenders, existing loans to hospitals from those lenders, and the resulting number of exposed hospitals, kept separate from the main outcome regression tables.

A separate matched analysis sample is constructed via nearest-neighbor matching on pre-period financial and mortality characteristics with a stated precision caliper, used throughout as a parallel robustness sample alongside the full sample.

The main treatment indicator is defined at the individual hospital-lender relationship level: it switches on once at least one of a hospital's relationship banks has undergone a stress test as of the prior year, rather than being defined at the hospital-system level.

The outcome set spans financial performance, operational utilization, risk-adjusted readmission and mortality measures, patient-survey ratings, and process-of-care timeliness indicators, with full variable definitions collected in a dedicated appendix table rather than only in table notes.

Financial ratios scaled by total assets are winsorized at a stated percentile in the main analysis, and a separate, less aggressive winsorization threshold is applied specifically for a profit-magnitude calculation elsewhere in the paper, with the difference explained in a footnote.
observations.locator: footnotes on control variables and Table 4 magnitude discussion

observations.statement: Many outcome and control variables enter regressions in natural-log form, including loan terms, bed-day capacity, and admission counts; the bed-day control is specifically transformed as log of one plus the count to accommodate zero values.

The paper identifies a specific measurement-consistency problem for one financial variable caused by a later change in reporting instructions that let hospitals retroactively restate prior-year figures, and excludes that variable from its time-series analysis as a result.

Main regression tables list included fixed effects and controls as indicator rows, report sample size and adjusted R-squared for every column, give the mean and standard deviation of the dependent variable, and state the standard-error clustering level in the notes paragraph rather than in the body text.

The main financing and operations table presents a baseline full-sample panel followed immediately by a second panel that reruns the identical specification on the propensity-score matched sample, keeping the same column layout across panels for direct comparison.

The loan-characteristics table progressively adds controls and fixed effects across adjacent columns, moving from a specification without controls to one that adds hospital controls plus loan-type and loan-purpose fixed effects.

One DRG-level admissions table reports both an unweighted specification and a companion specification that interacts treatment with a DRG-severity weight variable, placing the interaction coefficient directly beneath the uninteracted treatment row.

Standard-error clustering varies by the unit of observation across tables: loan-level regressions cluster at the lending-bank level while hospital-year and hospital-DRG-year regressions cluster at the hospital level, stated only in each table's notes.

Beyond stating the clustering level in table notes, the main text does not give an explicit econometric justification (such as the level of treatment assignment or serial-correlation concerns) for why standard errors are clustered at the chosen level in each table.

Parallel-trend figures for financial, utilization, readmission, mortality, and satisfaction outcomes are placed in the main text, plotting relative-year coefficients normalized to the exposure year with confidence bands, for both the full sample and the matched sample.

A footnote describes a formal statistical test of whether pre-period event-study coefficients differ from each other for each outcome, with outcomes that fail this test routed to a separate sensitivity-bounds analysis detailed in the online appendix.

A pre-period summary-statistics table reports hospital characteristics separately for the full sample, the treatment group, and the control group, functioning as an informal balance check; a companion footnote reports tests of the matching variables in the matched subsample.

As a diagnostic against known biases in two-way fixed-effects staggered DID estimates, the paper reruns its event-study analysis with an estimator designed for staggered adoption and heterogeneous treatment timing, comparing the resulting plots and treatment-effect estimates to the baseline.

A placebo check compares treated hospitals against untreated hospitals located in the same city, intended to probe whether local, non-credit shocks could explain the results; the test is summarized narratively in the main text with full results deferred to the online appendix.

Subsample robustness checks rerun the main specifications separately on for-profit hospitals, hospitals in small systems, hospitals that took out new loans after exposure, and hospitals with commercial-bank borrowing, summarized narratively with most supporting tables placed in the online appendix.

The paper reports that results are qualitatively similar when control variables are dropped entirely and when the staggered treatment definition is replaced by a single post-period indicator interacted with a static pre-period exposure dummy.

As an alternative to the baseline two-way fixed-effects staggered DID, the paper implements an estimator built for staggered adoption settings and reports that the resulting average treatment-on-treated estimates and event-study plots are similar to the baseline.

For outcomes whose pre-trend test is rejected, the paper applies a bounding approach that asks how much a post-period estimate could be explained by an assumed violation of parallel trends, reporting that inferences remain valid under the stated conservative assumptions.

The paper reports robustness to adding a hospital-type fixed effect for hospital categories otherwise excluded from the sample, and to adding region-by-time fixed effects intended to absorb time-varying local shocks.

The robustness subsection explicitly states that it only briefly summarizes checks in the main text and that considerably more detail is provided in the online appendix, so most robustness tables referenced are not reproduced in the paper itself.

Heterogeneity in hospital responses is estimated through interaction terms between the treatment indicator and hospital-level moderators such as ex ante bank-loan reliance, for-profit status, market power, and cash holdings, within the same two-way fixed-effects specification as the main results.

Treatment intensity is further split by how close a hospital's lenders' stress-test outcomes were to the regulatory capital threshold, interpreting closer proximity to the threshold as indicating a more severe credit shock and testing for a correspondingly stronger response.

All heterogeneity cuts are explicitly framed as tests of the hypothesized credit-supply channel: the paper states an ex ante prediction of where responses should be stronger before presenting each interacted specification.

Coefficient magnitudes are repeatedly expressed as a share of the dependent variable's unconditional sample mean, including for readmission-rate and process-of-care coefficients, to give readers a sense of economic size beyond the raw regression units.

Several coefficients are converted into aggregate dollar or patient-count terms through a stated back-of-envelope calculation, such as translating an interest-rate coefficient into additional yearly interest expense per hospital and a utilization coefficient into additional patients accommodated, with the arithmetic shown in a footnote.

The readmission-rate magnitude is benchmarked against the documented effect size of an unrelated federal readmissions-reduction policy program to argue that the paper's estimated effect is large relative to an established policy comparison point.

Profit and revenue effects are translated into monetary terms and compared against each other in the text, used to argue that internally generated funds rose by more than the direct increase in the cost of debt.

The paper acknowledges that mortality-rate observations are frequently missing for some conditions because many hospitals do not report them, and that mortality for slower-progressing conditions may not manifest within the sample's post-treatment window, and narrows its primary mortality analysis accordingly.

The paper treats the general concern that two-way fixed-effects staggered DID estimates can be hard to interpret as a caveat about the baseline specification specifically, addressed by rerunning the analysis with an estimator designed for staggered adoption rather than by abandoning the baseline design.

The paper cautions that documenting an operational shift after the shock does not necessarily imply hospitals were previously operating suboptimally, instead framing the change as a reoptimization between profitability and a health-provision objective under tighter financial constraints.

Parallel-trend figures use a coefficient-plot layout with the exposure year normalized to a reference value of zero and confidence bands drawn around each relative-year point estimate, applied consistently across financial, utilization, and quality outcomes.
The paper includes a map showing the count of exposed hospitals by geographic referral region, used to visually support the argument that treated hospitals are not concentrated in particular areas.

Every regression table's notes paragraph follows a consistent format: it states the standard-error clustering level, defines each outcome variable in prose, and lists which fixed effects and controls are included in that column.

The paper places two distinct summary-statistics displays early in the data section: one on the yearly distribution of tested lenders and exposed hospitals, and a separate one on hospital-level financial and operating characteristics split by treatment status.

The introduction previews the paper's full chain of results in narrative form, including the credit-supply effect, the financing and operating response, the quality-of-care decline, the mechanism evidence, and the heterogeneity and robustness findings, before any formal section begins.
The introduction closes with an explicit roadmap paragraph that names each subsequent numbered section and its topic before transitioning into the institutional background section.
observations.quote: The remainder of this paper is organized as follows

observations.statement: The introduction contains several dedicated paragraphs positioning the paper against multiple distinct literatures, including financial constraints, real effects of credit shocks, hospital finance, and treatment-rate variation in health care, before the empirical design is introduced.
Within the research-design section, the data and summary-statistics discussion precedes the formal presentation of the empirical specification and estimating equation.

The mechanism analysis is placed in its own section after the main results section and is explicitly framed in its opening paragraph as explaining the previously documented main effects using supplementary microdata.

Heterogeneity and robustness checks are consolidated into a single dedicated section following the mechanisms section, rather than interleaved with the main results tables, and that section explicitly defers most supporting detail to the online appendix.

Rather than describing data and code access directly in the main text, a title-page footnote directs readers to the article's official online page for additional materials and author disclosure statements.
observations.quote: additional materials and author disclosure statement(s)

observations.statement: The reference list cites a dedicated data-and-code deposit for the paper with its own persistent identifier, alongside multiple named source datasets, some public-use and administrative and others commercial or licensed, without a consolidated in-text data-availability statement describing access terms for each.

The main text describes specific access conditions for restricted inputs, noting that loan and hospital-affiliation records required a manual borrower-to-hospital match, while the government cost-report and quality data are described as accessed through public agency and research-mirror channels.

concordance.paper_says: Text describes a staggered difference-in-differences panel regression with hospital and year fixed effects (equation 1); no software command is named in the main text.
concordance.card_shows: Card records estimator hdfe_ols via Stata command reghdfe for s1/s2/s3.
concordance.note: Substance matches (linear panel FE regression); paper does not name the software command, card supplies it from code.

concordance.paper_says: Equation (1) and table notes state hospital and year fixed effects are included in the main specification.
concordance.card_shows: s1 and s2 record fixed_effects = [hos_id, year].

concordance.paper_says: Table 4 and Table 5 notes state standard errors are clustered at the hospital level.
Table 3 notes state loan-level regressions cluster standard errors at the lender level, distinct from the hospital-level clustering used elsewhere.
concordance.card_shows: Card has no specification entry for the Table 3 loan-level regression; only s1-s3 (hospital-year and event-study specs) are recorded, all clustered at hos_id.
concordance.card_ref: specifications (no record for Table 3 loan-level spec)
concordance.note: The lender-level clustering choice for the loan-facility analysis is not represented anywhere in the card.

concordance.paper_says: Text names the two lagged hospital-level controls used throughout the main specification as log of one plus available bed days and cash holdings over total assets.
concordance.note: Paper text resolves the card's unresolved control_var symbol.

concordance.paper_says: Text states the hospital-year sample covers a period beginning in 2010, with most financial and utilization outcomes running through 2016 and readmission/mortality outcomes extended through 2017.
concordance.card_shows: pipeline.sample_restrictions record year>=2010, year<=2016 for s1/s2 scope and year<=2017 for s3 scope.
concordance.note: Card's restriction-to-spec mapping (s3 for the 2017 cutoff) is reversed relative to how the paper describes it (2017 cutoff applies to readmission/mortality, which the card labels s3 while the paper's Table 5 readmission spec is closer to card's s2); treated as a substantive agreement on the year ranges themselves.

concordance.paper_says: Text describes a DRG-level admissions table that interacts treatment with a DRG-severity weight variable as part of the mechanism analysis.
concordance.card_shows: s1/s2/s3 all record weights = null; no specification entry corresponds to the DRG-weight interaction table.
concordance.card_ref: specifications (no record for Table 7 weight-interaction spec)

concordance.paper_says: Text names CMS HCRIS cost reports, CMS Hospital Compare, HCAHPS, Dealscan, Federal Reserve stress-test results, HCUP State Inpatient Databases, IQVIA, and AHA affiliation data as data sources.
concordance.card_shows: Card's top-level data array is empty.

concordance.paper_says: Text describes the comparison group as hospital-year observations without a stress-tested relationship lender, and separately as never-treated or not-yet-treated hospitals for the staggered-adoption robustness estimator.
Text describes both a formal pre-trend equality test and event-study coefficient plots as parallel-trends checks.
concordance.card_shows: x1 (pretrend_test) and x2 (pretrend_plot) are recorded as observed/call_present with matching descriptions.

concordance.paper_says: Text describes implementing an estimator for staggered adoption settings (Callaway and Sant'Anna 2021) as a robustness check on the baseline two-way fixed-effects specification.
concordance.card_shows: robustness[0] records type alt_estimator, description citing the same Callaway and Sant'Anna (2021) doubly robust estimator.

concordance.paper_says: Text describes applying the Rambachan and Roth (2023) sensitivity-bounds approach for outcomes that fail the pre-trend test.
concordance.card_shows: robustness[1] records type sensitivity_bounds implemented via the honestdid Stata command.
concordance.note: Paper cites the method by its econometrics reference; card supplies the specific software implementation.

concordance.paper_says: Footnote 28 describes a matched sample constructed by matching treatment and control hospitals on 2011 values of cash over total assets, log bed days, patient revenue over total assets, and pneumonia mortality rate.
concordance.card_shows: robustness[2] records an alt_sample check using a probit match on patrev_ta, cash_ta, log_bedday, and est_pn_mort_rate in 2011.
concordance.note: Matching variables named in the paper correspond exactly to the probit covariates recorded in the card.

concordance.paper_says: Table 4 (financial/operational outcomes) and Table 5 (readmission/mortality outcomes) are the paper's tables corresponding to the main specification family.

gaps: No explicit econometric justification (assignment level, serial correlation) is given in the main text for why standard errors are clustered at the hospital level versus the lender level in different tables; the choice is only stated, not argued.
No statistical software package is named anywhere in the main text I read (the recipe card records Stata/reghdfe from the code, not from the paper itself).

No preregistration, pre-analysis plan, or IRB/ethics statement is present in the main text; the study uses secondary administrative and commercial data on hospitals rather than human-subjects data collection, which may explain the absence.

The online Appendix (Appendix A and Appendix B), referenced repeatedly for additional tables, figures, and robustness detail, is not part of the extracted text and could not be read; several robustness and heterogeneity claims are therefore only narrated in the main text without their supporting tables being directly observed.
No first-stage or weak-instrument diagnostics appear, consistent with the design being a difference-in-differences rather than an instrumental-variables strategy.

reading.note: Read the entire provided text (pages 1-46: title, abstract, introduction, institutional background, data and design, results, mechanisms, heterogeneity and robustness, conclusion, references). The paper refers extensively to an online Appendix (A and B) for additional tables, figures, and robustness detail; that online Appendix is not part of the extracted text and was not read.
